name: Urea

lead: Urea is a natural part of the skin's moisturizing factor and is used in creams to smooth rough, dry, scaly or bumpy skin, including dry body skin, keratosis pilaris texture and calloused heels.

It attracts and binds water as a humectant, and at higher concentrations it breaks down hydrogen bonds in keratin so thick scale loosens and sheds. A 2021 review describes its emollient, moisturizing, keratolytic, barrier-enhancing and antimicrobial properties, and it has a long record in dermatology.

paras: People apply urea creams or lotions to the body, elbows, knees and feet once or twice daily, with lower strengths for general dryness and higher strengths for thick, scaly areas. Softer skin is often noticeable within days to a couple of weeks. Facial use is less common.

Mild stinging is the main side effect, especially on cracked or inflamed skin and at higher strengths. It is available without a prescription in most markets. Facial anti-aging use has been little studied.

angle.text: Urea creams are used for rough, dry or bumpy skin on the body and feet, and sometimes for keratosis pilaris texture. Urea draws in and holds water and loosens dead scale, so skin feels and looks smoother. Its moisturizing and keratolytic role is well established in dermatology.

lead: Urea (carbamide, CO(NH2)2) is a colorless, odorless, water-soluble compound that is the main nitrogen-containing end product of protein metabolism in mammals, formed in the liver through the urea cycle and excreted in urine. It is practically non-toxic, and most industrial production goes to fertilizer [1]. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler showed that urea could be made from inorganic starting materials, a milestone in the history of chemistry [1].

For appearance, urea matters as a skin-care ingredient. It is a natural component of the skin's moisturizing factor, and creams and lotions containing it are used to hydrate dry skin, soften rough or scaly patches on the feet, hands, elbows and legs, and smooth thickened skin such as calluses and keratosis pilaris, which can leave skin looking more even and feeling smoother [2][3][4]. Reviews describe a concentration-dependent pattern: at about 10 percent or less urea mainly moisturizes, and above that it also loosens and sheds thickened outer skin cells [2][3].

A 2021 review in Dermatology and Therapy describes its emollient, moisturizing, keratolytic, skin barrier enhancing and antimicrobial properties, and a 2018 review in Dermatologic Therapy covers its use in skin care [2][3]. A US label for a 40 percent urea cream lists indications including dry rough skin, xerosis, ichthyosis, eczema, psoriasis, keratosis pilaris, corns and calluses, and damaged or ingrown nails [4]. Wikipedia also notes urea as an ingredient in some hair conditioners and shampoos and as the main active in chemical hair removers [1].
Forum mentions of urea mostly concern blood urea as a laboratory marker, discussed in bodybuilding communities, rather than skin creams [5][6][7].
infobox: Topical creams, lotions, shampoos and nail products; oral/IV in specific medical uses
Roughly 2 to 10 percent for moisturizing; 10 to 30 percent moisturizing with keratolytic action; 30 percent and above for thick skin and nails [2]
About 180 million tonnes capacity in 2020; over 90 percent fertilizer [1]

paras: Urea creams are used for rough, flaky or cracked skin on the feet, hands, elbows and body, and are marketed for bumpy skin such as keratosis pilaris. Low concentrations are described as moisturizing, while higher concentrations soften thick scale and calluses [2][3][4].

Wikipedia notes urea in skin creams, moisturizers, hair conditioners and shampoos, and as a main ingredient in hair-removal creams [1]. The 2021 review lists the formats in which it is made: creams, lotions, ointments, gels, shampoos and nail lacquers, a flexibility that comes from its high water solubility [2].

A US 40 percent urea cream label lists debridement and promotion of healing of hyperkeratotic lesions, including where healing is slowed by infection, necrotic tissue or debris, and states that urea is useful in conditions such as dermatitis, psoriasis, xerosis, ichthyosis, eczema, keratoderma, corns, calluses and diseased nails [4]. Wikipedia describes 40 percent urea under an occlusive dressing as a nonsurgical way to remove diseased nail plate [1].

The 2021 review summarises uses in xerosis (including elderly, diabetic and hemodialysis patients), atopic dermatitis, ichthyosis, psoriasis, palmoplantar keratoderma, hand-foot skin reaction, radiation dermatitis, scalp seborrheic dermatitis, actinic keratosis pretreatment, nail disorders and tinea pedis [2].

Urea is also studied in other medicine. Registered trials examine oral urea for hyponatremia caused by SIAD or subarachnoid hemorrhage and oral urea as a stimulus in testing polyuria-polydipsia [8][9][10][11]. Wikipedia notes use as a diuretic from 1892 onward and the blood urea nitrogen test as a marker of kidney function [1].

The 2021 review sorts topical urea into low (about 2 to 10 percent), medium (about 10 to 30 percent) and high (30 percent and above) strengths, with moisturizing and barrier support at the low end, combined moisturizing and keratolytic effects in the middle, and debridement of thick plaques, nails and localized hyperkeratosis at the top [2]. Celleno's 2018 review uses a similar cut-off, describing mainly moisturizing action at 10 percent or below and keratolytic action above it [3].
Because urea can increase the penetration of other drugs, the reviews describe combinations with corticosteroids, antifungals and other agents [2][3].

The 2021 review summarizes multiple lines of evidence for emollient, moisturizing, keratolytic, barrier-enhancing and antimicrobial properties [2]. It reports studies of mostly 10 percent urea in xerosis, a 5 percent urea product associated with 37 percent lower relapse risk in one atopic dermatitis randomized trial, and improvement of flaking and roughness with a 10 percent formulation in ichthyosis vulgaris trials [2].

In a registered phase 3 trial, 12 percent ammonium lactate was compared with 10 percent urea cream in 40 older adults with xerosis [12]. A randomized trial of 216 patients receiving capecitabine compared usual care with usual care plus a urea-based cream; any-grade hand-foot syndrome occurred in 62.4 percent of the usual-care group and 56 percent of the cream group, a difference the authors reported as not statistically significant, with a tendency to milder syndrome in later cycles [13]. The 2021 review separately describes 10 percent urea reducing sorafenib-related hand-foot skin reaction in randomized trials [2]. A phase 2 trial tested topical diclofenac for the same syndrome [14].

The US label for a 40 percent urea cream lists transient stinging, burning, itching or irritation as adverse reactions that normally disappear when use stops, and warns for topical use only and to avoid contact with eyes, lips and mucous membranes [4]. The 2021 review describes urea as generally well tolerated, with mild, temporary irritation more likely at high concentrations and occasional temporary odor; it notes allergic contact dermatitis has been reported only rarely [2]. Wikipedia describes urea as practically non-toxic, while noting it can irritate skin, eyes and airways in some conditions [1].

Topical urea is described as binding water as a humectant and, at higher concentrations, as loosening hydrogen bonding in keratin to help shed dead skin, with reported effects on barrier function and antimicrobial peptide expression [2][3]. The 2021 review reports that in keratinocytes urea upregulates genes for filaggrin, loricrin and transglutaminase-1 and raises antimicrobial peptides such as cathelicidin and beta-defensin-2, lowers transepidermal water loss, and moves through the skin via urea transporters and aquaporins [2]. It also reports that urea slows epidermal cell turnover in a way that can thin the epidermis [2].
Physiologically, urea is produced in the liver from ammonia and carbon dioxide and plays a central role in nitrogen excretion; the kidneys reabsorb some to help concentrate urine [1].

Urea is the simplest amide of carbamic acid and is dissolved in water as a neutral solution. More than 90 percent of industrial production goes to agriculture as a nitrogen fertilizer [1]. The name comes from the Greek word for urine [1].

Herman Boerhaave obtained urea in 1727 by evaporating urine, and Hilaire Rouelle is credited with isolating crystals in 1773 [1]. Wöhler's 1828 synthesis, from silver cyanate and ammonium chloride, is often cited as an early laboratory synthesis of an organic compound from inorganic materials and challenged the doctrine of vitalism [1]. Industrial production relies on the Bosch-Meiser process, patented in 1922, which forms ammonium carbamate that decomposes to urea and water [1]. The 2021 review notes that topical urea has long been used in traditional medicine and for wounds [2]. A 2014 review covers urea's biochemistry [15].

On T Nation, urea is discussed mainly as a blood test result. Users post lab panels showing urea or BUN, and others describe urea as a product of protein breakdown after training or high protein intake [5][6][7]. These threads concern physiology and lab interpretation, not skin products.
Beyond skin care, Wikipedia lists uses in animal feed, diesel exhaust fluid, de-icing and food processing, and as a protein denaturant in laboratories [1].

Topical urea has been studied in dry skin and in oncology supportive care. Studies include the 40-participant ammonium lactate versus urea cream trial in xerosis [12], a 216-patient randomized trial of urea cream for capecitabine hand-foot syndrome [13], and a registered phase 2/3 trial with the same aim [16]. Reviews summarize the broader dermatology literature [2][3].

Other human work concerns systemic urea: terminated and ongoing trials for hyponatremia [8][9][11], a copeptin study in healthy adults and patients with polyuria-polydipsia [10], and the urea-to-creatinine ratio as a biomarker of catabolism in critical illness [17]. These are unrelated to cosmetic use.

timeline.event: Herman Boerhaave obtains urea by evaporating urine. [1]
Hilaire Rouelle is credited with obtaining urea crystals from urine. [1]
Friedrich Wöhler synthesizes urea from inorganic starting materials. [1]
Urea begins to be studied as a diuretic. [1]
The Bosch-Meiser process for industrial urea production is patented. [1]
Celleno publishes a review of topical urea in skin care. [3]
A review of urea in dermatology covers its emollient, keratolytic and barrier effects. [2]
A randomized trial of urea-based cream for capecitabine hand-foot syndrome is published. [13]
